questions.question: What is a database index?

options.text: A data structure that improves query speed by providing quick lookup paths

questions.explanation: An index is a data structure (typically B-tree or hash) that allows the database to find rows without scanning the entire table. Like a book index—jump directly to relevant pages instead of reading everything.

questions.question: What is the trade-off of adding indexes?

options.text: Faster reads but slower writes and more storage

questions.explanation: Indexes speed up reads but slow down writes (index must be updated on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) and consume storage. Over-indexing hurts write performance. Index strategically based on query patterns.

questions.question: Which columns are good candidates for indexing? (Choose all that apply)

options.text: Columns frequently used in WHERE clauses
Columns with high cardinality (many unique values)

questions.explanation: Index columns used in WHERE, JOIN, and ORDER BY. High cardinality (many unique values) makes indexes effective. Low cardinality (few values like boolean) or rarely-queried columns don't benefit much from indexing.

questions.question: What is a composite (compound) index?

options.text: An index on a single column
An index on multiple columns, useful for queries filtering on those columns together

questions.explanation: Composite index covers multiple columns (e.g., (last_name, first_name)). Efficient for queries filtering on those columns together. Column order matters—index on (A, B) helps queries on A or (A, B), but not B alone.

questions.question: A query filters on columns A and B. An index exists on (A, B). Which queries can use this index? (Choose all that apply)
questions.explanation: Composite index (A, B) follows leftmost prefix rule: it helps queries on A alone or (A AND B). Query on B alone can't use this index efficiently. OR conditions typically can't use single composite index well.

questions.question: What is a covering index?

options.text: An index that covers the entire table
An index containing all columns needed by a query, avoiding table lookup

questions.explanation: Covering index includes all columns a query needs. The query can be satisfied entirely from the index without accessing the table (index-only scan). Significantly faster for read-heavy queries.

questions.question: True or False: Primary keys are automatically indexed in most databases.
questions.explanation: Most databases automatically create an index on the primary key. This ensures fast lookups by primary key and enforces uniqueness. Foreign keys, however, are often NOT automatically indexed.

questions.question: What is index selectivity?

options.text: The ratio of distinct values to total rows—higher is better

questions.explanation: Selectivity = distinct values / total rows. High selectivity (close to 1) means the index effectively narrows down results. Low selectivity (e.g., boolean column) means index doesn't help much—still scans many rows.

questions.question: A table has 10 million rows. A query without index takes 30 seconds. With a proper index, approximately how fast might it be?
questions.explanation: Indexes can reduce query time from seconds to milliseconds by avoiding full table scans. B-tree index lookup is O(log n)—for 10M rows, only ~24 comparisons needed. Dramatic improvement for selective queries.

questions.question: What is a partial (filtered) index?

options.text: An index on a subset of rows matching a condition
An index on part of a column

questions.explanation: Partial index only includes rows matching a condition (e.g., WHERE status = 'active'). Smaller than full index, faster to maintain. Useful when queries consistently filter on the same condition.

questions.question: Which situations indicate missing or ineffective indexes? (Choose all that apply)

options.text: Full table scans in query execution plans

questions.explanation: Signs of missing indexes: EXPLAIN shows full table scans, queries slow on large tables, high disk I/O for reads. Fast performance indicates indexes are working. Use EXPLAIN to analyze query plans.

questions.question: What is index fragmentation?

options.text: Index pages becoming non-contiguous and less efficient over time due to updates

questions.explanation: As data is inserted/updated/deleted, index pages become fragmented (non-contiguous, partially filled). This increases I/O and slows queries. Periodic index rebuilding or reorganization addresses fragmentation.
